Developmental surveillance uses milestones as a guide, recognizing the range of normal. By about 2 months infants smile socially; by 6 months they sit with support, roll over, and babble; by 9 to 12 months they pull to stand, wave, use a pincer grasp and say "mama" and "dada" specifically, and by 12 months show stranger anxiety and respond to name; at 12 to 15 months they walk independently; by 18 months they have at least several words, and by 2 years they combine two words, run and follow two-step commands; by 3 years they speak in short sentences understood by strangers and ride a tricycle; and by 4 to 5 years they hop, draw a person, tell stories and cooperate in play. Primitive reflexes (Moro, rooting, palmar grasp) fade in the first months, and persistence beyond that suggests neurologic abnormality. The AAP recommends standardized developmental screening at 9, 18 and 30 months, and autism-specific screening at 18 and 24 months (for example with the M-CHAT-R/F). Red flags requiring evaluation include loss of previously acquired skills (regression), no babbling by 12 months, no words by 16 months, no two-word phrases by 24 months, and lack of social engagement. Hearing screening is performed in newborns, and vision screening is done at periodic intervals, with concern for amblyopia (treated by patching or atropine) and strabismus.

Newborn screening detects metabolic and genetic conditions such as phenylketonuria, congenital hypothyroidism, cystic fibrosis, sickle cell disease and congenital heart disease (by pulse oximetry), through blood spot and other testing, and early treatment prevents intellectual disability and death. Anticipatory guidance changes with age: safe sleep (supine position, a firm separate sleep surface and no soft bedding to reduce sudden infant death syndrome), breastfeeding support, introducing complementary foods around 6 months (including early introduction of peanut-containing foods in infants with severe eczema or egg allergy under guidance, to reduce peanut allergy), avoiding cow's milk as a main drink until 12 months and honey until 12 months (infant botulism), car seat use (rear-facing as long as possible within the seat's limits), water safety, firearm storage, limits on screen time and dental care. The USPSTF recommends fluoride supplementation for children over six months whose water is deficient, and application of fluoride varnish to primary teeth. Iron-deficiency screening is performed around 12 months, and lead screening is based on risk. Lipid screening once between ages 9 and 11 and again between 17 and 21 is recommended by AAP guidance, although the USPSTF finds insufficient evidence.

Adolescent care emphasizes confidentiality, which supports honest disclosure and is balanced by safety and reporting duties. The HEADSS or HEEADSSS interview (home, education and employment, eating, activities, drugs, sexuality, suicide and depression, safety) structures the psychosocial history. Screening includes depression (the USPSTF, 2022, grade B, recommends screening ages 12 to 18, and the AAP advises doing so annually), suicide risk (for which the USPSTF finds the evidence insufficient to assess screening), substance use, sexually transmitted infections and HIV in those with risk or after age 15, and attention to eating disorders, bullying, intimate partner violence and sexual exploitation. Contraception and vaccination (HPV, meningococcal, Tdap) are central. The leading causes of death in adolescents are unintentional injury, suicide and homicide, so helmet use, seat belts, avoidance of impaired driving and counseling on firearm safety are core preventive services. Puberty onset is assessed with Tanner staging: thelarche (breast budding) is the first sign in girls, usually at 8 to 13 years, followed by menarche about two to two and a half years later, and testicular enlargement is first in boys at 9 to 14 years. Precocious puberty (before age 8 in girls and 9 in boys) and delayed puberty (no breast development by 13 or testicular enlargement by 14) warrant evaluation.

Worked example: a 15-month-old girl has no words, does not point and does not respond to her name, with normal hearing screening at birth. This warrants audiology referral, developmental and autism screening, and early intervention services without waiting.

questions.prompt: Which term describes protecting patients from unnecessary or harmful medical interventions?
choices: Tertiary prevention, which limits complications of established disease
Quaternary prevention, which guards against overmedicalization
Primary prevention, which prevents the onset of disease
Secondary prevention, which detects early disease in the asymptomatic

questions.prompt: Why is the pretest probability of a serious disease lower in primary care than in a referral clinic?
choices: Patients present earlier and with less differentiated symptoms
Primary care patients as a group have fewer chronic diseases than hospital patients
Primary care clinicians refuse to order diagnostic tests
Serious diseases are never first seen by family physicians

questions.prompt: A 22-year-old woman has a rare condition with a 1 in 10,000 prevalence. A screening test has 95 percent sensitivity and 95 percent specificity. Why would most positive results still be false?
choices: The sensitivity is too low to detect disease at that rate
Specificity falls whenever prevalence decreases
Tests with 95 percent sensitivity always overcall disease when the condition is uncommon
The low prevalence makes the positive predictive value very low

questions.prompt: A man says he does not want to decide about prostate screening alone, and asks the clinician what to do. Which response best reflects shared decision-making?
choices: Tell him that screening is useless and should never be done
Defer the decision entirely to his spouse without discussion
Describe benefits and harms, ask about his values, and decide together
Order the test immediately because screening is always protective in men of his age group

questions.prompt: A patient with chronic low back pain reports new urinary retention and numbness around the perineum. What is the most appropriate step?
choices: Opioid analgesics and watchful waiting at home this week
Urgent evaluation, including MRI, for cauda equina syndrome
Reassurance and a trial of conservative care for six weeks
Referral to physical therapy and a follow-up visit in one month

questions.prompt: What does lead-time bias do in a screening program?
choices: Detects cancers that never would have caused symptoms
Recruits healthier volunteers than the general population
Lengthens apparent survival without delaying death
Selects slow-growing tumors that are less lethal

questions.prompt: At what ages does the 2021 USPSTF recommend colorectal cancer screening as a grade A or B?
choices: 40 to 70, with every adult in that range graded A and screened by colonoscopy yearly
50 to 85, with no distinction between age subgroups
55 to 80, with annual colonoscopy as the only option
45 to 75, with 45 to 49 graded B and 50 to 75 graded A

questions.prompt: A 52-year-old woman smoked one pack daily for 30 years and quit one year ago. Which recommendation best fits her?
choices: Annual low-dose CT lung cancer screening
Annual chest radiography for lung cancer
No lung screening because she has quit smoking
Single low-dose CT only at age 65

questions.prompt: A 26-year-old woman has had normal cytology results. What is the recommended interval according to the 2018 USPSTF?
choices: No screening until age 30
Cytology every three years
Cytology every year indefinitely
High-risk HPV testing alone every five years

questions.prompt: A 72-year-old man asks for a PSA test for prostate cancer screening, and he has a 15-year life expectancy. What is the USPSTF position?
choices: Recommends an individual decision after age 70 only
Recommends digital rectal examination alone every year
Recommends against routine screening at age 70 and older
Recommends screening annually with PSA testing for all men through age 85

questions.prompt: Which test is recommended to confirm an elevated office blood pressure before diagnosing hypertension?
choices: A repeat office reading at the same visit only
A resting electrocardiogram
A plasma renin level
Ambulatory or home blood pressure monitoring

questions.prompt: A 58-year-old man with diabetes, a 10-year risk of 12 percent and no prior cardiovascular events asks about a statin. What is the USPSTF recommendation?
choices: A statin is recommended only if the LDL is above 190 mg/dL
Aspirin is preferred over statins for all primary prevention
A statin is recommended for adults 40 to 75 with a risk factor and a risk of 10 percent or more
A statin is not recommended for primary prevention unless he has already had a myocardial infarction

questions.prompt: A 67-year-old man, a former smoker, has no symptoms. Which screening is recommended once?
choices: Resting ECG for coronary disease
Abdominal ultrasound for aortic aneurysm
Carotid duplex ultrasound for stenosis
Echocardiography for ventricular function

questions.prompt: A 49-year-old woman with a 10-year cardiovascular risk of 8 percent has borderline risk and prefers to avoid a statin if possible. Which test may help refine the decision?
choices: Coronary artery calcium score
Exercise stress echocardiogram
Carotid intima-media thickness in all patients
A resting electrocardiogram

questions.prompt: A 63-year-old man with no cardiovascular disease asks to start daily aspirin for prevention. What does the 2022 USPSTF recommend?
choices: Starting aspirin for all adults older than 60 with hypertension
Starting aspirin only in those with a family history of colon cancer
Starting aspirin in all adults above age 40 who smoke
Not initiating aspirin for primary prevention at age 60 or older

questions.prompt: Which vaccine is contraindicated in pregnancy?
choices: Measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, which is a live attenuated vaccine
Tetanus, diphtheria and acellular pertussis vaccine, given in every pregnancy
Inactivated influenza vaccine, given in any trimester during the season
Recombinant hepatitis B vaccine, given when the person is at risk

questions.prompt: Why are polysaccharide vaccines conjugated to a protein carrier?
choices: To delay antigen release and prevent injection-site pain
To produce a T-cell-dependent response with immune memory in young children
To convert the polysaccharide vaccine into a live attenuated formulation that replicates
To avoid the need for an adjuvant in all adults

questions.prompt: A 16-year-old has no immunization records and arrives for a sports physical. Which approach is correct?
choices: Defer all vaccines until laboratory immunity testing is done for each disease
Give only tetanus and defer all others until adulthood
Give age-appropriate catch-up doses, counting any documented doses and using minimum intervals without restarting series
Restart every vaccine series from the beginning because records are missing, then repeat all doses

questions.prompt: A 6-year-old develops a mild cold with a low-grade fever and is due for MMR and DTaP. Which statement is correct?
choices: Any fever at all is a contraindication until the child has been fully well for a full week
Antibiotic use is a contraindication to live vaccines
MMR can only be given after a negative measles antibody test
Mild illness with low-grade fever is not a contraindication to vaccination

questions.prompt: A 62-year-old man with no history of shingles asks whether he should get the recombinant zoster vaccine. What is the recommendation?
choices: Yes, two doses are recommended for adults aged 50 and older
No, it is recommended only for adults over 80 years of age
Yes, but the live zoster vaccine is preferred in older adults
No, it is recommended only after an episode of shingles

questions.prompt: Which test is recommended once for all adults aged 18 to 79 according to the 2020 USPSTF?
choices: HPV DNA testing
Hepatitis C antibody testing
Hepatitis A IgM testing
Herpes simplex type 2 serology

questions.prompt: Which group does the USPSTF recommend screening for chlamydia and gonorrhea?
choices: Sexually active women aged 24 and younger, and older women at increased risk
All men aged 15 to 30 irrespective of sexual activity, with annual urine testing
All women over age 40 with no risk factors
Only people with symptoms of urethritis or cervicitis

questions.prompt: A 29-year-old with a positive interferon-gamma release assay has a normal chest radiograph and no symptoms. What is the best management?
choices: Begin four-drug therapy for presumed active tuberculosis while awaiting sputum cultures
Repeat the test in a year without treatment
Perform lung biopsy to confirm infection
Treat latent tuberculosis, such as with four months of rifampin

choices: Syphilis only if the partner has had a positive test
Herpes simplex serology, hepatitis E antibody and cytomegalovirus IgM for every patient
HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B surface antigen and rubella immunity
HIV and hepatitis A only, with others based on symptoms

questions.prompt: A 27-year-old woman is planning a pregnancy. Which supplement does the USPSTF recommend daily to prevent neural tube defects?
choices: Vitamin E at 400 units daily
Folic acid, 0.4 to 0.8 mg
Vitamin A at high daily doses
Iron at 100 mg of elemental iron

questions.prompt: Which class of antihypertensive can cause a dry cough because of bradykinin accumulation?
choices: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers
Beta-blockers
ACE inhibitors
Thiazide diuretics

questions.prompt: Which is a contraindication to ACE inhibitors and ARBs?
choices: Diabetes with albuminuria
Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
Prior myocardial infarction
Pregnancy

questions.prompt: A 28-year-old woman has hypertension, hypokalemia and a low renin. What is the best next test?
choices: Plasma aldosterone-to-renin ratio
Plasma free metanephrines level
Renal artery duplex ultrasound alone
Thyroid-stimulating hormone with free T4

questions.prompt: A 55-year-old man with a repeated reading of 152/94 and no comorbid disease needs treatment. Which initial regimen is reasonable?
choices: Spironolactone as the only agent in uncomplicated disease
A single-pill combination of two first-line classes, with lifestyle changes
A beta-blocker alone, since it has been the traditional first-line agent for all patients
An ACE inhibitor combined with an ARB for stronger effect

questions.prompt: A 52-year-old man with diabetes has an LDL of 130 mg/dL and no cardiovascular disease. What does the 2026 ACC/AHA dyslipidemia guideline recommend?
choices: A fibrate as the first-line agent
Niacin to raise HDL cholesterol
Statin therapy, as for all adults with diabetes aged 40 to 75
No lipid therapy until a cardiovascular event occurs

questions.prompt: Which drug class slows kidney disease progression and reduces heart failure hospitalization in people with type 2 diabetes?
choices: Sulfonylureas, which increase insulin secretion from the pancreas
Thiazolidinediones, which improve insulin sensitivity in fat tissue
DPP-4 inhibitors, which prolong incretin hormone activity
SGLT2 inhibitors, which reduce glomerular hyperfiltration

questions.prompt: A GLP-1 receptor agonist is contraindicated in which condition?
choices: Established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease together with diabetes
Obesity with a body mass index above 35 and prediabetes
Medullary thyroid carcinoma or multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2
Chronic kidney disease with albuminuria in a patient with diabetes

questions.prompt: A 60-year-old man with type 2 diabetes on metformin has an eGFR of 48, albuminuria and an A1c of 7.8 percent. Which addition is most appropriate?
choices: Discontinuation of all renin-angiotensin blockers in order to protect the kidney function
An SGLT2 inhibitor, while continuing an ACE inhibitor or ARB for albuminuria
A sulfonylurea, since it has the strongest renal protection
Pioglitazone, since it lowers albuminuria without risk of edema

questions.prompt: A 70-year-old with type 2 diabetes, advanced heart failure and limited life expectancy has an A1c of 7.9 percent on stable therapy. What is the most reasonable approach?
choices: Accept a less stringent target, around 8 percent, to avoid hypoglycemia
Intensify therapy to reach an A1c below 6 percent
Stop all glucose-lowering medication immediately
Switch to a basal-bolus insulin regimen aimed at reaching a normal fasting glucose

questions.prompt: Which is a classification feature of chronic kidney disease?
choices: A creatinine rise lasting about a week in the setting of acute illness with dehydration, without albuminuria
A urinary tract infection that recurs more than twice a year
Kidney stones recurring in a patient with normal eGFR
Abnormal kidney structure or function lasting longer than three months, staged by eGFR and albuminuria

questions.prompt: Which description fits the diagnostic finding of COPD on spirometry?
choices: Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio below 0.70
Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio above 0.90
Reduced total lung capacity with a normal ratio
A 12 percent rise in FEV1 after bronchodilator

questions.prompt: Why is a long-acting beta agonist never used alone in asthma?
choices: It lowers the efficacy of the short-acting reliever
It treats bronchospasm but not inflammation, and increases severe event risk
It causes severe hypokalemia and arrhythmia in all patients who take it regularly
It is only effective in combination with oral steroids

questions.prompt: A 35-year-old woman uses albuterol daily and wakes at night with cough. What is the most appropriate management change?
choices: Start a long-acting beta agonist alone as the new controller
Begin daily oral corticosteroids as long-term controller therapy
Step up to an inhaled corticosteroid-formoterol regimen after reviewing technique and triggers
Increase albuterol to four times daily as the main strategy for her symptoms

questions.prompt: A 62-year-old man with COPD has two exacerbations in a year and a blood eosinophil count of 400 cells per microliter. Which addition has the best rationale?
choices: Long-term daily oral prednisone to prevent exacerbations in all patients
Theophylline as the first add-on agent
Stopping bronchodilators to reduce adverse effects
An inhaled corticosteroid added to dual long-acting bronchodilators

questions.prompt: A 40-year-old woman has fatigue, weight gain and constipation, with a TSH of 14 mIU/L and low free thyroxine. What is the best treatment?
choices: Levothyroxine, adjusted by TSH in six to eight weeks
Methimazole to suppress thyroid hormone production and reduce gland activity
Radioactive iodine to ablate the gland
Observation with repeat testing in a year

questions.prompt: Which body mass index range defines obesity in most adults?
choices: 40 or higher only
30 or higher

questions.prompt: Which weight-loss drug is contraindicated in patients with a seizure disorder?
choices: Naltrexone-bupropion
Semaglutide
Orlistat
Tirzepatide

questions.prompt: A 45-year-old woman with a body mass index of 33 and prediabetes asks about weight loss. What is the best approach?
choices: Advice to simply eat less and exercise more, with no structured program or follow-up
Bariatric surgery referral as the first and only option
A single-nutrient supplement and reassessment in a year
Intensive multicomponent behavioral therapy, with discussion of pharmacotherapy

questions.prompt: A 50-year-old man who underwent Roux-en-Y gastric bypass years ago has fatigue, a macrocytic anemia and paresthesias. Which deficiency is most likely?
choices: Vitamin K
Vitamin A
Vitamin B12
Vitamin C

questions.prompt: Which statement about dietary patterns in weight loss is supported by trials?
choices: Meal timing matters more than total energy intake for all people
Mediterranean, low-carbohydrate and low-fat diets produce similar weight loss when adhered to
Only very low-carbohydrate diets produce meaningful long-term weight loss in trials
Low-fat diets are consistently superior to all other patterns

questions.prompt: Which drug acts as a partial agonist at the alpha-4 beta-2 nicotinic receptor and is used for smoking cessation?
choices: Bupropion, which inhibits reuptake of norepinephrine and dopamine
Naltrexone, which blocks mu-opioid receptors in the brain
Nicotine gum, which delivers nicotine without combustion
Varenicline, which reduces craving and the reward from smoking

questions.prompt: What is recommended by the USPSTF for adults who use tobacco and are not pregnant?
choices: Electronic cigarettes as the first-line cessation aid
Medication only, with no counseling because it is ineffective
Behavioral interventions plus FDA-approved medication, which work better combined
Behavioral counseling alone, because medication adds no benefit to counseling in trials

questions.prompt: A 48-year-old man who smokes a pack daily says he is thinking about quitting someday. What is the best response?
choices: Document his statement and avoid pressuring him in any way
Advise him clearly, explore his motives and offer medication and counseling with follow-up
Tell him to return when he is fully ready to quit and offer counseling only then
Prescribe bupropion without discussion so he can use it when ready

questions.prompt: A 35-year-old woman has a seizure disorder and wants help quitting smoking. Which agent should be avoided?
choices: Bupropion, because it lowers the seizure threshold
Varenicline, because of high rates of psychosis
Nicotine patch, because it increases seizure frequency
Combination nicotine replacement, because of dependence risk

questions.prompt: A man with opioid use disorder asks about treatment. Which approach reduces mortality the most?
choices: Detoxification alone followed by outpatient follow-up
Counseling without any medication during the first year of treatment, then reassess
Short-term benzodiazepines to control withdrawal symptoms
Medication such as buprenorphine or methadone with counseling

questions.prompt: Which medication class is contraindicated with nitrates because of profound hypotension?
choices: 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors such as finasteride, which shrink the gland
Thiazide diuretics such as hydrochlorothiazide, which lower blood pressure
Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors such as sildenafil
Alpha-1 blockers such as tamsulosin, which relax prostate smooth muscle

questions.prompt: A man with benign prostatic hyperplasia takes finasteride. How does this change interpretation of his PSA?
choices: The PSA is raised by about half, so measured values are halved for interpretation purposes
The PSA becomes unreliable and should never be measured
The PSA is unchanged because the drug acts on testosterone only
The PSA is lowered by about half, so values are doubled for interpretation

questions.prompt: A 17-year-old has sudden severe left scrotal pain with nausea. The testis is high-riding and the cremasteric reflex is absent. What is the best next step?
choices: Immediate surgical exploration without waiting for imaging if suspicion is high
Oral antibiotics for presumed epididymitis with a follow-up visit in about a week
Scrotal ice and analgesics with outpatient ultrasound next week
Urinalysis and observation overnight in the emergency department

questions.prompt: A 24-year-old man has a painless, firm left testicular mass. What is the appropriate approach?
choices: Reassurance because testicular masses in young men are usually benign hydroceles
Scrotal ultrasound and tumor markers, followed by radical inguinal orchiectomy if suspicious
Transscrotal needle biopsy to confirm the diagnosis
Empiric antibiotics for two weeks and reassessment

questions.prompt: A 58-year-old man has fatigue and low libido and a low morning total testosterone twice, with low luteinizing hormone. What does this indicate?
choices: Normal aging that never requires evaluation
Androgen insensitivity syndrome
Secondary hypogonadism, which needs evaluation for pituitary or systemic causes
Primary testicular failure from an intrinsic testicular disorder with high gonadotropins

questions.prompt: Which contraceptive method is the most effective emergency contraception?
choices: Barrier method used afterward
Copper intrauterine device
Levonorgestrel pill
Combined oral contraceptive taken twice

questions.prompt: Which condition makes combined estrogen-progestin contraception category 4 (unacceptable risk)?
choices: Migraine with aura
Mild asthma
Previous gestational diabetes
Controlled hypothyroidism

questions.prompt: A 33-year-old woman smokes 20 cigarettes per day and has migraine with aura. She requests a combined pill. What is the best response?
choices: Prescribe the combined pill and counsel her to stop smoking before she starts it
Prescribe a higher-dose estrogen pill to improve her cycle control and reduce bleeding
Recommend no contraception because of her risk factors
Offer a progestin-only method or an intrauterine device instead

choices: Progestogen alone to treat vasomotor symptoms
Testosterone alone to treat vasomotor symptoms
Estrogen with a progestogen to protect the endometrium

An oral bisphosphonate taken upright with water, with calcium and vitamin D

Vitamin D supplementation for all older adults routinely
